Les Premières Nations et les Inuit du No: Will First Nations and Inuit in Northern Quebec feel represented after this election?
« Il est temps que les Inuit contrôlent: “It’s time for the Inuit to control their own destiny”
Pita Aatami et Mandy Gull-Masty. Photo f: Pita Aatami and Mandy Gull-Masty. Photo provided by Mandy Gull-Masty
Alors que les élections approchent à gra: With the election fast approaching, I want to shed light on a situation I became aware of while working at APTN. Most Inuit and Cree in Quebec live in a riding where their votes are often drowned out by non-Indigenous voters in the south.
J'ai pu réaliser une entrevue avec la se: I was able to interview the riding’s only Indigenous candidate, former Grand Chief Mandy Gull-Masty, at the start of her campaign, when she was passing through Montréal. She committed to prioritizing Indigenous concerns if elected. I would have liked to speak with the other candidates in person, but I was only able to do a phone interview with the NDP candidate. Because of travel costs – and the time required – I couldn’t interview any voters on the ground in Cree or Inuit territory. I phoned the Nunavik municipal offices to ask whether they wanted to talk about the election, as well as the Naskapi band office, but I got no response.
De nombreux dirigeants locaux se concent: Many local leaders are focused on looking after their communities rather than engaging in federal politics, where their voices often go unheard. I received a short message from Noah Swappie of the Naskapi Development Corporation, in which he says that “despite Trudeau’s recent reputation, First Nations have been better recognized than ever before [under his administration]. That’s my view.” That said, he was hesitant to comment on the election, and we did not do an interview, as he was busy devoting himself to his community. Federal elections don’t seem to be a priority in Naskapi territory – which seems logical, given that the Naskapi, Cree and Inuit populations make up only a third of the riding’s population.
J'ai voulu écrire sur ce sujet parce que: I wanted to write about this subject because First Nations and Inuit may have won the right to vote, but that doesn’t mean their vote counts as much as that of non-Indigenous citizens. Canada has introduced exceptions to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act regarding minimum population for certain provinces and territories (for example, Nunavut has its own riding and Prince Edward Island has four, all with fewer than 40,000 people). However, the distinct interests of certain Indigenous nations, such as taking traditional territorial boundaries into account, don’t seem to factor in when Canada designs these exceptions. This situation is little known among many Quebecers. I therefore hope this article will help explain Indigenous people’s frustration with the Canadian electoral system.
Les dirigeants des partis fédéraux tourn: Federal party leaders are turning their eyes north for mineral resources and Arctic security. But on the ground in Nunavik, Inuit leader Pita Aatami says his community’s votes will be buried under an avalanche of voters from the south.
Pita Aatami est président de <l1>la Soci: Pita Aatami is president of the <l1>Makivik Corporation</l1>, one of the governing bodies of Nunavik, an Inuit territory that stretches across northern Quebec and part of Labrador. The electoral map for Nunavik (Abitibi-Baie-James-Nunavik-Eeyou) discourages Inuit from voting in Canadian federal elections, he says with regret.
« À chaque élection, on se demande toujo: “Every election, we always wonder what’s going to happen, because we don’t have the population needed to get a member elected to Parliament,” he explains.
Le Nunavik fait partie de la plus grande: Nunavik is part of the largest electoral riding in Quebec by area, which spans 700,000 km<sup>2</sup>. In the north, the riding of <l1>Abitibi-Baie-James-Nunavik-Eeyou</l1> includes the Cree and Naskapi First Nations located in Quebec and the Inuit of Nunavik. Farther south, there are a few Anishinaabe communities such as Lac-Simon and Kitcisakik – and a few non-Indigenous towns, such as Val D’Or and Senneterre.
Avec les Cris d'Eeyou-Istchee et les Nas: Together, the Cree of Eeyou Istchee, the Naskapi near Labrador and the Inuit of Nunavik in the riding of Abitibi-Baie-James-Nunavik-Eeyou number 32,900 people, out of a <l1>total population of about 90,000</l1>. <l2>For years</l2>, these Cree, Naskapi and Inuit have been campaigning for their own riding.
Selon eux, ils forment une communauté d’: According to them, they form a community of interest, which could justify the creation of a separate electoral riding, <l1>according to the ACE Electoral Knowledge Network</l1> (of which Elections Canada is a contributing partner).
« Pendant de très nombreuses années, la: “For a great many years, the Inuit’s conduct was dictated to them. So it’s time for the Inuit to control their own destiny,” says Pita Aatami.
« Pourquoi ? Pourquoi sommes-nous traité: “Why? Why are we treated differently? We want equality,” he insists.
La Commission de délimitation des circon: The Electoral Boundaries Commission says it is respecting Canadian law
The Federal Electoral Boundaries Commission for Quebec heard the request for a northern riding during the public consultations held in 2022.
Selon Louis Massicotte, un des trois mem: According to Louis Massicotte, one of the three members of the <l1>Quebec commission</l1> in 2022-2023, the Commission chose not to create this new riding because the population concerned was too small, and the redistribution would have had repercussions for voters farther south.
« Dans ce cas-ci, franchement, la demand: “In this case, frankly, the request made to us had consequences
assez énormes sur le plan de l'égalité d: that were quite enormous in terms of voter equality. And that’s the reason [we did not approve it],” says Mr. Massicotte.
Le raisonnement de la commission est éla: The commission’s reasoning is set out in <l1>its report</l1> (for more information, see the box at the bottom of the article).
Si les Premières Nations et les Inuit au: If First Nations and Inuit in northern Quebec were to get their own riding, the redistribution commission would be obliged to find a riding to absorb the 60,000 voters south of the current boundaries. If they joined the neighbouring riding of Abitibi-Témiscamingue, it would then include more than 140,000 people – so the power of their votes would be weakened.
Essentiellement, Massicotte explique que: Essentially, Massicotte explains that to create a riding in northern Quebec, Canadian law would have to be amended and a proposal would have to be submitted outlining how the impacts in the south could be managed.
Selon lui, la commission a été à l’écout: He says the commission listened to Indigenous people. “I think there has never been a commission as favourable to Indigenous people as ours. The fact that about a dozen Indigenous names were added to the names of Quebec ridings, one for each nation in Quebec, was not something Indigenous people asked for. It was an initiative of the commission.”
Mais Pita Aatami souligne que les différ: But Pita Aatami points out that the differences between the southern communities and the northern Indigenous communities should have justified creating their own riding.
« Nous sommes très distincts. Nos réalit: “We are very distinct. Our realities are very different from those of our neighbours and the issues they may have. The cost of living is a problem we’ve been facing for a long time. Overall, we’ve benefited from support from both governments, but we’re still not at the same level as the rest of Canada. I will always fight to be treated on an equal footing. I’m a citizen, a taxpayer. I want the same benefits as my fellow Canadians,” says Mr. Aatami.

Parmi ses priorités figurent l'améliorat: Her priorities include improving access to traditional food (food from hunting or gathering in the region), community engagement, improving infrastructure and the economy, and addressing the lack of services in Cree and Inuit communities.
« Il y a des lacunes dans les services [: “There are gaps in [health] services for people from a northern community,” she laments. “I have two little cousins. They’re autistic. Sa plus grande priorité est sans doute l: Her biggest priority is arguably the economy. The Liberal Party has pushed for increased resource development, <l1>including through oil and gas pipelines</l1>, to boost the Canadian economy. As Grand Chief, Ms. Gull-Masty says she learned to walk a tightrope between respecting Indigenous rights in order to protect their traditional territories and the openness of some of them to development.

You have to be able to understand where the balance lies between these two points of view,” she explains.
« J'ai remporté un <l1>prix internationa: “I won an <l1>international award</l1> for being recognized as a visionary leader in the field of environmental protection. During my career, I also developed businesses <l2>tied to mining projects</l2>,” Ms. Gull-Masty points out.

La députée du Bloc québécois Sylvie Béru: Bloc Québécois MP Sylvie Bérubé has visited Nunavik only twice since she was elected in the riding in 2019, and has met Pita Aatami only once.
Dans une entrevue accordée à <l1>Nunatsi: In an interview with Nunatsiaq News, Ms. Bérubé said she would visit Nunavik “a little more often, at least once or twice a year” if re-elected. The Bloc Québécois did not respond to La Converse’s interview request.

« C'est une bonne chose que les libéraux: “It’s a good thing that the Liberals chose an Indigenous candidate, but it’s not enough when you look at the party’s record and compare it to that of the NDP, which has always had a much stronger plan to make Indigenous voices heard,” he says.
Il qualifie les avancées des libéraux su: He describes the Liberals’ progress on Indigenous issues as “piecemeal”: <l1>the Liberal government has been spinning its wheels</l1> on missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, and has only <l2>recently advocated</l2> for <l3>strong northern infrastructure</l3>, such as increased investment in housing and electricity, he believes.
En cas de victoire, il militera pour la: If he wins, he will push for the creation of a riding in northern Quebec and will oppose Bill 96, Quebec’s language law, which many Indigenous groups oppose, particularly English-speaking and Inuktitut-speaking Inuit. “It was the NDP caucus that, under Ed Broadbent’s leadership, pushed for the inclusion of Indigenous peoples in the Constitution,” he recalls.
Dans les années 1980, le député néo-démo: In the 1980s, NDP MP <l1>Ed Broadbent did indeed refuse</l1> to sign on to Pierre Trudeau’s constitutional reforms unless Indigenous rights were included. That refusal helped lead to the inclusion of <l2>Section 35</l2>, which recognizes Indigenous treaty rights and inherent rights.

« Il y a eu des meurtres d'Autochtones e: “There have been killings of Indigenous people and youth because the RCMP is taking repressive measures. Selon Élections Canada, chaque circonscr: According to Elections Canada, each riding in Quebec must have approximately 108,998 people (what is called the “electoral quota”) and the province is to have a maximum of 78 ridings in 2023, as set out in the representation formula of Canada’s Constitution Act. Members of redistribution commissions do not have the power to change the number of electoral ridings.
À l’exception de « <l1>circonstances ext: Except in “<l1>extraordinary circumstances</l1>,” the population of ridings must not deviate by more than 25% from the electoral quota, and the commissions aim for a 0% deviation. For the northern communities covered in this article, creating a riding of 30,000 people would result in a deviation of 72% from Quebec’s electoral quota (108,998). A riding that included voters from the south of the current riding and from Abitibi-Témiscamingue would exceed the quota by 28%.
Quelques exceptions inscrites dans la lo: There are a few exceptions written into Canadian law: the territories each have their own riding, even though these ridings do not have the required population. Each province must have as many ridings in the House of Commons as it has senators. Prince Edward Island has four senators, and therefore four ridings, despite a population of fewer than 40,000 people.
